title: Agnello alla Pignata
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Lamb slow-braised in a traditional terracotta pot with tomato, onion, and pecorino, the earthenware vessel said to lend the finished stew a uniquely earthy, mellow depth.
longDesc: Pignata refers to the rounded terracotta cooking pot itself, historically set directly into the embers of a wood fire, and Basilicata cooks maintain that this specific vessel genuinely changes the character of the finished stew compared to cooking in metal.
ingredients: 1.2 kg (2.6 lb) lamb shoulder, cut into chunks
80 ml (1/3 cup) extra virgin olive oil
Salt and chili flakes, to taste
equipment: Terracotta pot (pignata) or heavy Dutch oven with lid
steps: Warm the olive oil in the pignata or a heavy pot and brown the lamb pieces on all sides.
Add the onions and garlic, and saute until softened.
Pour in the wine and let it reduce.
Add the crushed tomatoes, potatoes, rosemary, and chili flakes, and enough water to nearly cover the ingredients.
Cover and cook over very low heat for 2-2.5 hours, until the lamb is completely tender.
Stir in the grated pecorino in the final 10 minutes, letting it melt into the sauce.
Season to taste and serve hot, directly from the pot if using a traditional pignata.
chefTips: If using a genuine terracotta pignata, cook over the lowest possible heat, as these vessels can crack under high or uneven heat.
The low, slow cooking is essential for both the lamb tenderness and the sauce depth of flavor.
Stirring in the pecorino at the end thickens the sauce naturally without needing any flour or cream.
commonMistakes: Cooking a terracotta pot over high heat, which risks cracking it.
Rushing the braise, leaving the lamb tough rather than properly tender.
Adding the pecorino too early, which can cause it to separate rather than melt smoothly into the sauce.
servedWith: A robust red wine from Basilicata
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days; flavor improves the next day.
reheating: Reheat gently on the stovetop, covered.
healthBenefits: A good source of protein and iron from the lamb.
culturalNote: Agnello alla pignata is closely tied to the traditional terracotta cooking vessel it takes its name from, a method still practiced in parts of rural Basilicata.
